Future projections are based on the 2024 UN's medium-fertility scenario. Chart created by [[Our World in Data|Our World In Data]] in 2024.]]
{{Short description|None}}This article contains a '''list of countries by past and projected future population'''. This assumes that countries stay constant in the unforeseeable future, and does not take into account possible border changes. 

==Overview==
All the figures shown here have been sourced from the International Database (IDB) Division of the [[United States Census Bureau]]. Every individual value has been rounded to the nearest thousand, to assure data coherence, particularly when adding up (sub)totals. Although data from specific statistical offices may be more accurate, the information provided here has the advantage of being homogeneous.

Population estimates, as long as they are based on recent censuses, can be more easily projected into the ''near'' future than many [[macroeconomics|macroeconomic]] indicators, such as [[gross domestic product|GDP]], which are much more sensitive to political and/or economic crises. This means that [[demography|demographic]] estimates for the next five (or even ten) years can be more accurate than the projected evolution of GDP over the same time period (which may also be distorted by [[inflation]]).

However, no projected population figures can be considered exact. As the IDB states, "figures beyond the years 2020–2025 should be taken with caution", as the "census way towards those years has yet to be paved". Thus projections can be said to be looking through a kind of "cloudy glass"<ref>Britannica Book of the year 2003, [[Encyclopædia Britannica]] Publishers, [[Chicago]], 2002, page 779.</ref> or a "misty window": realistically, the projections are "[[guesstimate]]s".

To make matters more complicated, not all countries carry out censuses regularly, especially some of the poorer, faster-growing [[sub-Saharan Africa]]n nations (whose evolution may be more interesting, from a demographer's point of view, than the "stagnated" populations of countries like [[Germany]] or [[Italy]]). The populations of many of these countries, as well as other primarily [[Muslim population growth|conservative, Islamic]] nations like [[Egypt]], [[Iraq]], and [[Pakistan]], are growing much faster due to their high [[fertility rate]]s than in the [[population ageing|aging]] [[Europe]]an nations or [[Japan]].

On the other hand, some other countries, like the small [[Asia]]n state of [[Bhutan]], have only recently had a thorough census for the first time: In Bhutan's case in particular, before its national 2005 population survey,<ref>[http://www.citypopulation.de/Bhutan.html Bhutan on the CityPopulation website].</ref><ref>[http://www.geohive.com/cntry/bhutan.aspx Bhutan on www.geohive.com]</ref><ref>[http://www.statoids.com/ubt.html Bhutan on Statoids.com]</ref> the IDB estimated its population at over 2 million; this was drastically reduced when the new census results proved to be  672,000.

Further, the IDB usually takes some time before including new data, as happened in the case of Indonesia. That country was reported by the IDB to have an inflated population of some 242 million by mid-2005, because it had not still processed the final results of the 2000 Indonesian census.<ref>[http://www.bps.go.id/eng/tab_sub/view.php?tabel=1&daftar=1&id_subyek=12&notab=1 1971, 1980, 1990 and 2000 Indonesian censuses] (and 1995 intercensus count), on the ''Badan Pusat Statistik'' (BPS, Statistics Indonesia) website.</ref><ref>[http://www.cipypopulation.de/Indonesia.html Indonesia on CityPopulation].</ref><ref>[http://www.geohive.com/cntry/indonesia.aspx Indonesia on GeoHive.com] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091015060224/http://www.geohive.com/cntry/indonesia.aspx |date=2009-10-15 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.statoids.com/uid.html Indonesia on Statoids]</ref> There was a similar discrepancy with the relatively recent [[Ethiopia]]n 2007 census,<ref>[http://www.citypopulation.de/Ethiopia.html Ethiopia on CityPopulation]</ref><ref>[http://www.geohive.com/cntry/ethiopia.aspx Ethiopia on GeoHive] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120805184429/http://www.geohive.com/cntry/ethiopia.aspx |date=2012-08-05 }}</ref> which gave a preliminary result of "only" 73,918,505 inhabitants.

The largest absolute potential discrepancies are naturally related to the most populous nations. However, smaller states, such as [[Tuvalu]], can have large ''relative'' discrepancies. For instance, the 2002 census in that [[Oceania]]n island, which gave a final population of 9,561<ref>[http://www.spc.int/prism/country/tv/stats/Census%20&%20Surveys/Census_index.htm Central Statistics Division - Government of Tuvalu - Census of Population and Housing and sample Surveys], on the Pacific Regional Information System (PRISM), within the Secretariat of the Pacific Community (SPC) website.</ref> shows that IDB estimates can be significantly off.

==Preliminary notes==
The national 1 July, mid-year population estimates (usually based on past national censuses) supplied in these tables are given in thousands.

The retrospective figures use the present-day names and world political division: for example, the table gives data for each of the 15 republics of the former [[Soviet Union]], as if they had already been independent in 1950. The opposite is the case for [[Germany]], which had been divided since the end of the [[World War II|Second World War]] but was [[German reunification|reunified]] on October 3, 1990.

Other issues concerning some countries or territories are as follows:

*{{Flagicon|MMR}} Burma is the [[names of Myanmar|traditional English name for (the Union of) Myanmar]], as used by the [[United States Census Bureau]].
*{{Flagicon|COD}} The [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], formerly known as Zaire from 1971 to 1997, is referred to as Congo (Kinshasa) in the IDB database (to differentiate it from the [[Republic of the Congo]] whose capital is the city of [[Brazzaville]]).
*{{Flagicon|FRA}} The population figures for [[France]] include the five [[overseas departments and regions of France|overseas departments]] of [[French Guiana]], [[Guadeloupe]], [[Martinique]], [[Mayotte]], and [[Réunion]], but exclude [[Saint Barthélemy]] and the French part of [[Collectivity of Saint Martin|Saint Martin]], which split from Guadeloupe in 2007.
*{{Flagicon|HKG}} {{Flagicon|MAC}} The former [[United Kingdom|British]] colony of [[Hong Kong]] and former [[Portugal|Portuguese]] colony of [[Macau]] continue to have their own figures, even though they returned to [[China|Chinese]] sovereignty in 1997 and 1999 respectively. The Chinese government considers both these present-day Special Administrative Regions (SARs) as separate entities from a statistical point of view, and their censuses are still carried out on different dates from mainland China.
*{{Flagicon|MSR}} About half the population of the [[United Kingdom|British]] [[Caribbean]] colony of [[Montserrat]] (in the [[Lesser Antilles]]) was evacuated in 1995, following a [[types of volcanic eruptions|volcanic eruption]] that severely damaged its capital, the town of [[Plymouth, Montserrat|Plymouth]].
*{{Flagicon|PSE}} Although no figures are given for the [[Palestinian territories]] as a whole, data is supplied for both the [[Gaza Strip]] and the [[West Bank]].
*{{Flagicon|SRB}} The [[Serbia]]n population refers only to that of the "residual" Yugoslav republic under that name, after secession of [[Montenegro]] ''(Crna Gora)'' and, more recently, [[Kosovo]] (the latter being recognized as an independent state by the [[federal government of the United States|United States government]] on 18 February 2008, the [[United States Census Bureau|U.S. Census Bureau]] reflects the resulting [[demography|demographic]] change; nevertheless, many countries have not recognized this declaration of independence).

Finally, the [[Eastern Europe|Eastern]] and [[Western Europe]] subtotals follow the former [[Cold War]]'s [[Iron Curtain]] division of Europe.

==Formulas used to calculate demographic growth==
To the right of each year column (except for the initial 1950 one), a percentage figure is shown, which gives the ''average annual'' growth for the previous five-year period. Thus, the figures after the 1960 column show the percentage annual growth for the 1955-60 period; the figures after the 1980 column calculate the same value for 1975–80; and so on.

The formulas used for the annual growth rates are the standard ones, used both by the [[United Nations]] Statistics Division and by National Census Offices worldwide. They are [[compound interest|compound growth rates]], and have the general form:

<big><math>\left ( \sqrt[y_f-y_i]{\frac{p_f}{p_i}} -1 \right ) \times 100</math></big>

where <math>p_i</math> and <math>p_f</math> stand for the initial and final population, respectively, within a stated time period. Similarly <math>y_i</math> and <math>y_f</math> are the dates of the initial and final years.

In the calculations shown here, all periods are of five years, so{{space|2}}''y''<sub>''i''</sub> + 5 = ''y''<sub>''f''</sub>{{space|2}}and the formula simplifies to:

<big><math>\left ( \sqrt[5]{\frac{p_f}{p_i}} -1 \right ) \times 100</math></big>.

The Medium variant of the forecast for July 1, 2024, July 1, 2030, July 1, 2050 and July 1, 2100 is given.<ref>{{cite web|title=Compact (most used: estimates and medium projections) (XLSX, 24.07 MB)|url=https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Files/1_Indicators%20(Standard)/EXCEL_FILES/1_General/WPP2022_GEN_F01_DEMOGRAPHIC_INDICATORS_COMPACT_REV1.xlsx|website=|date=2022|accessdate=2023-12-12|lang=en|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007114649/https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Files/1_Indicators%20(Standard)/EXCEL_FILES/1_General/WPP2022_GEN_F01_DEMOGRAPHIC_INDICATORS_COMPACT_REV1.xlsx|archivedate=2023-10-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=World Population Prospects - Population Division - United Nations|url=https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Standard/MostUsed/|website=|accessdate=2023-12-12|lang=en|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20231205201116/https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Standard/MostUsed/|archivedate=2023-12-05}}</ref>

==External links==
*[https://population.un.org/wpp United Nations - Department of Economic and Social Affairs - Population Division - World Population Prospects 2024] provides official UN estimates and projections of country populations 
*[http://www.citypopulation.de/ City population] provides [[demography|demographic]] data ''not'' only for cities, but also for countries (and their primary administrative divisions), sometimes going back to the 1980s.
*[https://web.archive.org/web/20090129161316/http://geohive.com/earth/his_proj.aspx GeoHive page] with historic, current and future population by country, also based on the United States Census Bureau International Data Base.
*[https://web.archive.org/web/20150223080259/http://www.populstat.info/ Population statistics] has a collection of [[demography|demographic]] statistics from every country and territory, some of them going back ''centuries''.
*[http://www.statoids.com/ Statoids] gives historical and present-day census data about countries and territories, and figures for their first (and even second) level administrative divisions.
*{{webarchive |date=2012-12-04 |url=https://archive.today/20121204142112/http://www.world-gazetteer.com/ |title=World gazetteer}} includes present-day national population projections, going back to the 1990s in some cases.
*[http://www.ifs.du.edu/ifs/Ifs.aspx International Futures] (IFs) is an integrated global modeling system that forecasts demographic, economic, energy, agricultural, socio-political, and environmental subsystems for 183 countries interacting in the global system.
